Greek Tragedy. The dominant literary form of ancient Athens, primarily during the fifth century BCE, in which playwrights explored themes of fate, human suffering, divine justice, and moral consequence through dramatic narratives featuring noble or legendary figures. Performed at religious festivals like the City Dionysia, these plays established the fundamental structures and conventions—protagonist, chorus, tragic flaw, catharsis—that have defined drama for over two millennia.

The form emerged in the sixth century BCE and reached its peak in the Classical period around the middle of the fifth century, when Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides dominated Athenian theater. Performances were part of religious festivals, most notably the City Dionysia, dedicated to the god Dionysus, where playwrights competed for prizes and prestige. The typical structure included a chorus, a group of actors commenting on the action, episodes featuring principal characters, and stasimon, which are choral odes. Plays were performed in day-long trilogies or groups.

Central to the form was the concept of the tragic flaw, called hamartia in Greek—a character's fatal mistake or moral blindness leading to inevitable downfall and suffering, often culminating in recognition, or anagnorisis, and reversal, or peripeteia. Aristotle later codified tragedy's rules in the Poetics, defining catharsis—the purification of audience emotion through pity and fear—as the form's purpose. Women and slaves, though excluded from performing or attending, were frequently the subjects of drama, with female characters often embodying transgression, passion, or divine retribution. The three great tragedians—Aeschylus with The Oresteia and Agamemnon, Sophocles with Oedipus Rex and Antigone, and Euripides with Medea and The Bacchae—left fewer than fifty surviving plays out of thousands originally written.

Aeschylus was the earliest of the three great tragedians and a pioneer of dramatic structure with multiple speaking actors. Sophocles was the master of the form, known for psychological complexity and exploration of destiny and human dignity. Euripides was an innovator who questioned divine justice and gave tragic voice to women, slaves, and marginal figures. Together, these playwrights established conventions that would shape Western drama for centuries to come.
